#1101. Breaking down the two controversial penalty incidents in Sunderland v Chelsea

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Enzo Le Fee scored the winner from the spot after Cole Palmer was denied at the other end

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It was a tale of two penalties at the Stadium of Light as Sunderland defeated Chelsea to move off the bottom of the Premier League.

First, Cole Palmer saw appeals waved away following a challenge from the side from Sunderland’s Luke O’Nien on the edge of the area.

Then, at the other end, Sunderland striker Brian Brobbey won a penalty when he went down under the challenge of Chelsea’s Levi Colwill.

Referee Jarred Gillett pointed to the spot and Enzo Le Fee converted to give Sunderland the lead and they held on to claim a vital victory.

Palmer, who was left out of England’s squad by Thomas Tuchel on Friday, had performed some superb skill to make space and dribble towards the box.

He got away from the challenge of Sunderland substitute Jules Ahoka, who had replaced injured captain Granit Xhaka, before O’Nien came in from the side.

O’Nien’s left leg appears to come across Palmer, crashing into him and bringing him down without touching the ball, but referee Gillett waved play on.

The incident was checked by VAR, however, with official Nick Hopton ruling that the contact between O’Nien and Palmer took place outside the area.

Palmer’s momentum meant he went down in the box, but the Premier League Match Centre confirmed that “any contact with Palmer occurs outside the penalty area.”

The Sunderland striker was a handful for the Chelsea centre-backs and Brobbey got a roll on Colwill to drive into the box.

Both players had a hold of each other as Brobbey turned. The Dutchman had his left arm on Colwill’s back while Colwill had his right arm on Brobbey’s shirt.

The contact continued as Brobbey entered the box, but what appeared to trip him up was when his right foot clipped his left and he tumbled to the ground.

The Chelsea players around Colwill immediately appealed, but Gillett pointed to the spot. Colwill may have also clipped Brobbey’s heels, but it was unclear.

Former Premier League referee Darren Cann told the BBC that Gillett was “spot on” to award the penalty, however.

”Brobbey and Levi Colwill were tussling outside the box and then it appeared there was lower leg contact on Brobbey which brought him down,” he said.

“Gillett was in the perfect position to see the infringement and award the penalty.”

Colwill was brought off at half-time, with Chelsea midfielder Moises Caicedo dropping into defence for Xabi Alonso’s side.

But Chelsea still fell to a fourth defeat in eight Premier League games as they failed to seriously threaten Sunderland in the second half.

The Black Cats had lost five of their previous six in the Premier League to fall to the bottom of the table, but claimed their first win in eight.

It relieves the pressure on under-fire Regis Le Bris ahead of the upcoming international break.

#1100. Inside the world of Captain Chaos at Man United: Michael Carrick will not walk away but here's what the players are saying as they fail to respond to his direction, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 02:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 08:52 EST, 9 November 2026

While the Manchester United fans who had gone ahead with a booze boycott of Old Trafford watched in horror as their team teetered on the brink of total collapse and head coach Michael Carrick clung to his job, you couldn't help but think of Lloyd Bridges as Steve McCroskey, the frazzled air traffic control boss in Airplane! 'Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit drinking!'

God knows United have forced their supporters to hit the bottle this season, not least in the past six days when they have handed a two-goal advantage to Roma and Aston Villa (twice) and still managed to salvage a win and a draw.

But this cannot carry on. As cavalier as United like to be, this is not the way to play football.

Coming out swinging every game like a boxer on his last legs is great for entertainment, it's great for the Sky Sports cameras beaming it live and the Amazon Prime documentary makers filming behind the scenes, but it is not evidence of solid preparation on the training pitch.

Nowhere in the UEFA coaching manuals will you find a chapter on routinely conceding the first two goals being a sensible route to success. For all his bluster after a bonkers 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, Carrick knows it and his players know it.

'After we concede goals we show character, but if we do this before we can win much more games,' said Matheus Cunha. 'I don't know why, everyone tries to get answers for that. We want to be the best and show that we can come back. We need to show the mentality to do this from the start.'

As Manchester United head coach, Michael Carrick is doing a convincing impersonation of Captain Chaos

Coming out swinging every game like a boxer on his last legs is great for entertainment, but it is not evidence of solid preparation on the training pitch

It isn't just in the last week either. United were a goal down against Atletico Madrid inside the first minute and Como in the second. They were two down to Villa after three minutes and 40 seconds, the earliest that has happened to United in the Premier League era.

This is not a coincidence. It is not bad luck. This is in the mind-set of these Manchester United players, and the game management of Carrick – and that is what should worry Old Trafford bosses the most.

As if being in the relegation zone for the next two weeks after a start of one win from 10 games – the worst since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago – is not bad enough, United don't seem to be playing to a plan. They are not responding to direction. They are reverting to instinct and moments of skill when everything else fails.

Carrick made reference to it when he spoke before this game, admitting that the players are better when they don't think too much.

'Momentum within games, day-to-day, week-to-week, game-to-game, it's huge,' he said at Carrington on Friday. 'I think it's important with your feelings and your emotions to roll with it. Then your memory can click in and you realise, 'Oh yeah, this is what it feels like, this is how it should be', and you start seeing different things.

'It's all got to come together, but feeling, confidence, and that emotion and sometimes not even thinking. You're at your best when you don't think too much and you just trust and play on instinct, and I think we did a lot of that the other night (against Roma).'

The irony is that Carrick was so measured, so composed as a player. Now, as coach, he is doing a convincing impersonation of Captain Chaos. United's games are reminiscent of the high-scoring madness of Erik ten Hag's last full season in charge, devoid of stability or structure.

That is what Carrick's employers need to consider when they sit down to discuss whether he can restore the sanity of his first four months in charge which guided the club towards third place and Champions League qualification.

Now they are third from bottom and will stay in the relegation zone for the duration of the international break. For three minutes on Sunday, Manchester United – the aristocrats of English football – were actually in last place after Sunderland took the lead against Chelsea and Crystal Palace were still goalless with Liverpool.

United don't seem to be playing to a plan or responding to direction - they are reverting to instinct and moments of skill when everything else fails

Carrick's employers need to consider  whether he can restore the sanity of his first four months in charge

That being in 18th place – one below Coventry – is somehow seen as blessed relief from the unrelenting humiliation of this season, says everything about the state of the club.

At the end of a week that marked 40 years since Ferguson's arrival and was celebrated by a dinner with many of his most famous players, it has been quite the fall from grace.

Which brings us back to the fans. They are a loyal bunch and once again serenaded Carrick off the pitch at full-time having spent much of the previous two hours slaughtering the owners, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

Protest groups had urged them to boycott buying alcohol at the stadium to hit the Glazer family and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in the pocket. 'Your funeral not ours – sell up now,' read one new banner. 'We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners,' said another.

But they know their football at United. Was it support or just sympathy with a head coach who has done his best in an impossible situation?

Carrick says he won't walk away and they never do. On Remembrance Sunday, he stood there on the touchline with a poppy on his arm and hope in his heart that United could get themselves out of another self-inflicted crisis.

They did. Again. But how much longer can United and Carrick keep winging it, and believe that calm will emerge from the chaos.

#1099. Brighton up to second in Premier League as Diego Gomez strike sparks comfortable win

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Brighton 1-0 Brentford: Gomez scored another stunning goal as his side rise to second in the table.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Diego Gomez scored another stunner as Brighton enjoyed a happy homecoming by climbing to second in the Premier League with a 2-0 win over 10-man Brentford at the Amex Stadium.

Albion have clocked up thousands of miles since thumping rivals Crystal Palace 5-0 three weeks ago, playing Conference League fixtures in Czechia and Spain either side of a trip to Liverpool and two visits to Manchester City.

Midfielder Gomez, who scored from the halfway line against Palace, rifled a thunderous, left-footed shot into the top left corner to give the high-flying Seagulls a 15th-minute lead.

Brentford striker Igor Thiago was sent off eight minutes later following a VAR review after catching Brighton midfielder Chema Andres in the face with a raised arm.

Pascal Gross sealed a comfortable victory for the hosts with a 42nd-minute penalty awarded for Keane Lewis-Potter’s shirt pull on Luka Vuskovic.

Albion’s win was a seventh from 10 top-flight games this term and lifted them above City and back to within five points of leaders Arsenal, while eighth-placed Brentford remain on 14 points.

Following Thursday’s 1-0 win away to Getafe, Brighton head coach Fabian Hurzeler reverted to the team which began the club’s maiden league victory at the Etihad Stadium last weekend.

His in-form side began on the front foot before edging in front in spectacular style.

Costinha’s cross from the right was only partially cleared by Bees defender Michael Kayode and Paraguay international Gomez took a couple of touches before unleashing an unstoppable effort high into the net from more than 25 yards.

Charalampos Kostoulas wasted a golden chance to add a quick-fire second by firing straight at Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

Brentford’s bid for a first Premier League win away to the Seagulls then became substantially harder.

Referee Michael Oliver initially booked both players after Brazil international Thiago reacted with annoyance to having his shirt pulled and then being pushed by Andres.

However, following a trip to the pitch-side monitor, Oliver upgraded Thiago’s punishment to red as he was deemed to have caught his opponent in the face “with force”.

Thiago, who earlier failed to seriously test Albion keeper Bart Verbruggen with a tame lob, left the pitch with a wry smile before Bees boss Keith Andrews endured further frustration.

Match official Oliver immediately pointed to the spot when Lewis-Potter impeded Vuskovic following a corner, leaving Gross to emphatically dispatch the penalty into the top-right corner.

Disgruntled away fans chanted “2-0 to the referee” and “Michael Oliver, it’s all about you” before watching their depleted team struggle to get out of their own half for large periods of a low-tempo second half containing a couple of flashpoints.

Brighton captain Lewis Dunk was booked for scything down Kevin Schade, prompting a disagreement with Brentford head coach Andrews.

Bees forward Schade received a yellow card of his own after a petulant shove on Vuskovic and was later unable to properly connect with a Callum Wilson cross.

Brentford were given five minutes of added time to make the home fans anxious but failed to register an attempt on target in the game as Albion eased to another three points.

#1098. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the big brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

The room is furnished in a typical Austrian style. Lots of wood, a fireplace, a few decorative touches. Through the large windows, you can see mountains surrounding the town of Saalfelden. Right on the dot, 21-year-old Jobe Bellingham arrives. It is August 2025, the midfielder has just signed for Borussia Dortmund and is giving his first press conference at the club’s training camp. German journalists are eager to find out what kind of character this talented youngster is. Will he provide any useful quotes for a story?

Half an hour later, the reporters are full of admiration and their notepads are full. Open-minded, self-assured, with clear opinions and a firm stance. That is how Bellingham presents himself. “It’s just not in my nature to be a superstar. I want to function like a machine,” he says. That was 15 months ago – a lot has happened since.

For his club, Bellingham is far more than just a midfielder. He is also a figurehead and a driving force behind the club’s marketing activities. The Bellingham name, made famous by his brother Jude, who played for Dortmund from 2020 to 2023 before moving to Real Madrid for almost €130m (£108m), is arguably the most recognisable in Dortmund’s squad. Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Ever since, the midfielder has enjoyed almost unwavering support. Watzke frequently spoke with him throughout his first season, offering encouragement and reassurance. The same was true of Kovac and other senior figures. Equally important to his breakthrough has been team-mate Felix Nmecha, with whom Bellingham has developed a close friendship and who has become an important source of advice. When time allows, the two enjoy playing padel together. Off the pitch they are opponents; on it they form a midfield partnership.

And while his father Mark was still complaining to club officials around a year ago that his son was not getting enough playing time, the situation has changed dramatically. The Bellingham family are delighted, and his England call-up has provided further confirmation that he is on the right path.

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

Green and gold balloons filled the Stretford End before kick-off, colours that look back to the club's past and signal rejection of the present leadership.

Chants against the Glazer family and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe rang out as the United players came out of the tunnel in front of the protest.

Many supporters had already made their feelings plain by that point. Opposition to plans for a new stadium that would replace Old Trafford was also voiced.

Many supporters are angry that money has gone on buying up land for the project rather than being invested in the squad.

Several fans groups had called on supporters to make their voices heard during the match. Their protest was directed at a decline in standards and a perceived attack on traditional fan culture.

United headed into Sunday’s match in 19th place in the Premier League table after Sunderland beat Chelsea 1-0 at the Stadium of Light earlier on Sunday afternoon.

Michael Carrick’s side then made a nightmare start to their game against Villa, with Unai Emery’s men scoring twice in the opening four minutes.

Alysson and Nicolas Jackson both found the net to put Villa in complete control, only for United to fight back for the second time in five days after their dramatic 3-2 win over Roma on Tuesday.

United captain Bruno Fernandes halved the deficit from the penalty spot, before Youri Tielemans equalised just before half time to ensure the hosts headed into the interval on level terms.

Villa retook the lead shortly after half time, though, with John McGinn scoring a penalty. Leon Goretzka then restored Villa’s two-goal-advantage shortly afterwards as United were made to pay for a slow start to the second half.

#1090. Toothbrush zaps bacteria with electricity that’s made when bristles move

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The history of the manual toothbrush has been traced back to the tenth-century Tang Dynasty in China. Credit: Valentyna Yeltsova/Getty

Researchers at Peking University in Beijing have developed a toothbrush in which bacteria are destroyed not only by mechanical friction, but also through an electrical charge that is generated by brushing. The work was published in Science Advances on 4 November1.

Generating electricity through brushing is a “new twist on an old concept”, says Frank Scannapieco, a periodontist at the University at Buffalo in New York. It might reduce plaque more efficiently than do conventional manual toothbrushes, although more tests are needed to prove efficacy and safety, he says.

The researchers showed that the brush did not damage the surface of the teeth and was not toxic to human cells, but they did not look at long-term safety or cost.

Bristled toothbrushes — which humans have used in various forms since the tenth century ad — rely mainly on motion to manually disrupt plaque, the film of bacteria, saliva and food particles that forms around teeth.

The team made the bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a polymer that they stretched and heated to obtain a piezoelectric form — meaning that it generated a charge when deformed.

When used to scrub teeth, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These molecules damage the cell membranes of bacteria in the plaque, say the researchers. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03586-y

Lu, Y. et al. Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg5744 (2026).

#1089. Wirtz breaks goalscoring duck as Liverpool send Palace boss closer to exit door

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool: Andoni Iraola’s side bounced back from two defeats on the spin but Palace, bottom of the table after 10 games, could now be forced to make a change in the dugout

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

For Andoni Iraola, at the end of a week of vexation following two avoidable one-goal defeats, this was just what the doctor ordered. On a cool November day, a comfortable margin of victory in second gear in South London halted Liverpool’s two-game losing run heading into the internationals and catapulted them back into the top-four, nine points off leaders Arsenal.

Even Florian Wirtz, Liverpool’s ultimate attacking fall guy over the last 15 months, netted a much-needed first Premier League goal of the season. Off a Bradley Barcola assist, too. Here at Selhurst, amid a forward quartet made up of just shy of £400m worth of transfer fees, there were more positive sprinklings of encouragement. And when Alexander Isak, who it should be said is second in the race for the golden boot with seven league goals, smashed the ball home on the cusp of 90 minutes, the three points were safe and heading back up to the north-west.

That said, this was all against a Crystal Palace side – and a manager in beleaguered Frenchman Pierre Sage – who by the end looked out of ideas and inspiration. No head coach has lost his job in the Premier League this season – yet – but the Eagles are now rooted to the bottom of the table after 10 games with just two wins to their name. Could a change be in the offing from Palace chairman Steve Parish, a man who does tend to afford managers time to put things right? We’ll find out soon enough.

Yet what will frustrate Sage the most on this occasion is that, until Liverpool’s second just after half-time, Palace were well in this match. But the team that has scored the second-fewest goals in the division (ten) were punished here for failing to take their chances in the first-half.

But a week on from failing to have a single shot on target against Arsenal, it took 20 seconds for Liverpool to find their range here as Mac Allister gave Dean Henderson an early test. The diminutive 5’9” midfielder, curiously effective from set pieces, went closer after 10 minutes, heading into the side netting from Dominik Szoboszlai’s free-kick. It was a warning and routine that Palace would not heed.

Yet after the first 15 minutes, Palace were the team on the ascendancy. Yeremy Pino’s neat swivel and shot crashed off the crossbar while Jogen Strand Larsen, in for the suspended Jean-Philippe Mateta, saw a dinked finish ruled out for offside, albeit correctly so.

And when Daichi Kamada gave Barcola a lesson in back-post volleys with a punchy effort kept out by Alisson, it was somewhat against the run of play when Mac Allister’s opener arrived.

Iraola had spoken in the build-up about his team perhaps being “too honest” as a statistic this week did the rounds: while Liverpool have conceded the most fouls in the Premier League, only three sides have won fewer fouls. But it pays to be shrewd. After Cody Gakpo won a questionably-given foul off Jefferson Lerma, Szoboszlai’s near-post free-kick was once again met by Mac Allister, who glanced sweetly home for his fifth goal of the season, equalling his tally from the last campaign.

His provocative celebration in front of the Holmesdale End only added to the home crowd's fury. “One-nil to the referee,” they sang at official Tony Harrington at the interval.

The Reds were, however, fortunate to be ahead at half-time. Their goal was under siege before the interval, with Quinten Timber and Adam Wharton forcing good saves out of Alisson. Palace’s momentum was stymied by the interval though and when Barcola’s square ball after a surge down the right found Wirtz, the German found the attribute he so often has been accused of lacking since his £105m arrival on these shores: composure. Stroking the ball beyond Henderson, it is just his sixth Premier League goal since arriving from Bayer Leverkusen last summer.

But even in the closing stages, Palace carved out decent opportunities. Pino somehow squandered a one-on-one opportunity with the goal gaping and substitute Eddie Nketiah poked over from close range. It was indicative of Palace’s fortunes: neat build-up, a large intake of breath in the box before failing to find the back of the net.

And when Isak put the icing on the cake, set up by Wirtz in the box and coolly cutting inside before lashing home past Henderson, Sage had the look of a man on the brink on the touchline. Even Milos Kerkez’s brainless foul on Dario Osorio in stoppage time, clattering the Palace substitute’s head in the box, which resulted in Nketiah’s consolation penalty and a needless ruining of Alisson’s clean sheet, could not brighten the Palace mood. Now, ahead of a two-week pause in action, the question for Parish is: will he stick or twist?

Leeds and the Premier League are launching an investigation into racist abuse and threats sent to Jayden Bogle’s family.

Bogle escaped a red card in the win over Tottenham after injuring Mathys Tel, with the Leeds full-back receiving the threats via social media.

Should Jason Bogle have seen red for this challenge? 🟥👀 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/fuK42Okkcz

His club have revealed they are looking to identify those who sent messages to the 26-year-old, whose family were threatened in one of the posts seen by Telegraph Sport after the 1-0 victory.

Leeds say they are “appalled at the disgusting, racist social-media abuse Jayden Bogle suffered” and will push for punishments to be taken.

The club added in a statement: “Leeds United condemns this behaviour in the strongest possible terms. There is no place for racism in football or society.

“The club will work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify the individuals and push for the strongest possible action to be taken against them.

“Jayden has the full and unconditional support of the club and his team-mates, and we all stand with him at this time. Nobody should ever be subjected to racist abuse.”

Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, described Bogle as the “softest player” in the Premier League who would never try to hurt an opponent.

Referee John Brooks did not issue a yellow card, with VAR Tony Harrington sticking with the on-field decision.

“I’m confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge,” Harrington was quoted on the big screen at Elland Road.

Tottenham will make a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to send off Bogle.

“I haven’t watched the scenes back so I can’t give you a clear opinion, out of the game it looked a handball but the scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench and it looked a very unlucky coming together,” Farke said.

“Fingers crossed for Mathys that he is back soon, but it looked like there was not much speed in this action, but Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the country, he would never injure or foul a player on purpose because he is such a fair character.”

Tottenham Hotspur’s purple patch of form ended with a worrying loss. Wearing their “Spurple” kit for the first time, Roberto De Zerbi highlighted a lack of character and personality from his players and refused to blame the defeat on referee John Brooks’s decision not to dismiss Jayden Bogle for leaving one of his players injured.

Spurs’ away strip is based on a 1990s design, but this performance was more Christian Gross than Jürgen Klinsmann or David Ginola. Leeds United created the better chances and eventually broke through with 11 minutes remaining when their substitutes combined for Noah Okafor to score the winning goal.

After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move Spurs into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

Bogle trod on his opponent’s foot before clattering into his knee, forcing the French forward off a few minutes later. “I know that Jayden doesn’t foul out of bad intentions, he is not a nasty player and is one of the softest players in the whole league,” Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said. “I call him my butterfly.”

De Zerbi admitted the injury was “bad” and that Tel would now be scanned to determine the extent of the problem. The Spurs boss was upset that Pedro Porro was later booked for a similar challenge, while Bogle went unpunished – but he said the referee was not the cause of the defeat.

“I was surprised because in the same position in the second half there were two different fouls, the yellow card for Pedro Porro is not possible. I don’t know if it is a red card or not on Mathys Tel but the parameter of the referee was not good enough for this in both situations,” De Zerbi said.

For Leeds, moving into the top half will lift their own hopes of challenging for Europe, such is the congested mid-table.

“For us it has been a difficult period, we are missing key players like Anton Stach, Noah, Dominic [Calvert-Lewin] has not had the easiest spell with several injury problems and it was important to show this unity and commitment to avoid all their individual quality to score goals and reduce them to very little,” Farke added.

“Our final third, the quality was perhaps not there but second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing for that win. Another clean sheet another terrific defensive behaviour.”

Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

Tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

#1085. Aston Villa boss Unai Emery storms down the tunnel after last-gasp Man United equaliser

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United trailed 4-2 in injury time at Old Trafford but rescued a point with a 4-4 draw and Villa boss Emery stormed down the tunnel after the goal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery appeared to storm off down the tunnel after Manchester United grabbed a last-gasp equaliser against his side to seal a remarkable 4-4 draw in one of the most chaotic Premier League games of the season.

United looked set for defeat as they trailed 4-2 in the second minute of injury-time at Old Trafford before Joshua Zirkzee gave them a sliver of hope by pulling one back and Patrick Dorgu headed home an incredible equaliser in the 96th minute.

That proved to be the final straw for Emery, who immediately stormed off down the tunnel without even waiting for the VAR check confirming the goal and before the full-time whistle blew for the end of the match.

In his post-match interview with Sky Sports, Emery suggested he simply left because United scored so late that he thought the match was essentially over.

Emery had already watched his side squander a 2-0 lead after the perfect start for the visiting Villans, with Alysson and Nicolas Jackson both finding the net inside the first five minutes.

That advantage didn’t last long as Matheus Cunha was fouled in the box by Boubacar Kamara and Bruno Fernandes stepped up to pull one back, sparking a period of constant pressure that continued until Youri Tielemans scored his first United goal to equalise against his former club before half-time.

Yet the hosts unravelled again however, as Villa scored twice in seven minutes after the restart, with John McGinn netting from the penalty spot after Diogo Dalot fouled Alysson and Leon Goretzka tapping in after more woeful defending from United.

At that point, Emery must have assumed his team would get over the line but they collapsed again with Zirkzee first pulling one back in the 92nd minute before Dorgu rose highest on 96 minutes to head into an empty net after Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki came off his line and failed to get the ball.

That result – combined with their incredible comeback victory against Roma in midweek – may just have saved Michael Carrick’s job, although his United side still head into this international break in the Premier League’s bottom three, lying 18th in the table.

Meanwhile, Villa’s rollercoaster start to the campaign means they are in 10th, although if they had held on for victory, they would have moved up to eighth.

#1084. Michael Carrick has painfully awkward exchange with interviewer over Man United future

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick appeared to be unimpressed by questioning from Sky Sports after United’s remarkable 4-4 draw with Aston Villa as he gave a series of terse responses

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick endured an awkward end to a post-match interview as he had an excruciating exchange about his future as Manchester United manager.

Carrick had just watched his United side fight back from 4-2 down in injury time to snatch the unlikeliest of 4-4 draws with Aston Villa, having earlier come back from being 2-0 behind inside five minutes.

It was a real mixed display from the Red Devils, who showed plenty of heart and character but had put themselves in bad positions due to consistently disastrous defending.

The result – combined with their incredible comeback victory against Roma in midweek – has probably saved Carrick’s job, although his United side still head into this international break in the Premier League’s bottom three, lying 18th in the table.

His long-term future appears to very much still be up in the air and his post-match interview on Sky Sports with reporter Patrick Davison was an awkward watch.

Carrick firstly bristled slightly when asked if United are looking at a relegation fight, saying: “No, we’re in November. I don’t like this situation we’re in, I don’t like the results we’ve had but we can definitely do something about it.”

From there, things got worse, as Davison asked a lengthy question suggesting there were clearly going to be conversations about his future during the international break over the next couple of weeks, to which Carrick simply responded: "Is there?"

When it was suggested that one would assume so, Carrick tersely said: “Would you?” and when he was pushed for what he thought about his situation, the Man United boss said to Davison: “You’re telling me, what do you think”.

After that, the interviewer specified that he wanted to know what Carrick expected to happen in the next couple of weeks and he then gave a longer answer admitting that it wasn’t a good situation, the team haven’t won enough games but that he expects to move forward and keep working on the things they’ve been working on until this point.

Back in the Sky Sports studio, pundit Roy Keane was asked for his thoughts on the interview as a whole and the former Man United midfielder compared the current boss to a politician.

He said: “It’s obviously difficult for the manager, he’s under pressure no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much – maybe that’s a tactic. He’s like a politician.

“He’s clearly under pressure and says he knows there are things to work on but he better get moving on that... This is their worst start in however many years.”

Keane was also critical of United’s “dreadful” defending, although he praised the heart they showed to twice come back from two goals behind.

He added: “I think we’ve said previously there have been question marks over this team but they’re showing a bit of fight, a bit of desire and, as bad as the game was from a footballing point of view, they kept going to the end.

“So, on the one hand, you say dreadful to give up four goals at home, but they kept going, so we have to give them a little bit of praise.

“In terms of the bigger picture, it’s that rollercoaster of watching United. Some bits were so, so bad. Defensively the way it started, the start of the second half, but they found a way to get a point in a game where they looked dead and buried.

“Still nowhere near good enough to try and get towards the middle of the table.”

#1083. Man United’s unique comeback leaves no one knowing how to feel

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa: Michael Carrick was applauded off as his players rescued an extraordinary draw, even though his side remained 18th in the Premier League and on an eight-game winless run

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As the Manchester United players who had been told they were not fit to wear the shirt, in perhaps the earliest ever airing of that chant in footballing history, celebrated a second ridiculous comeback in five days, the Stretford End launched into a different chorus.

They had told the team they were unworthy of representing them after a mere five minutes, had jeered in damning fashion when the dreadful Diogo Dalot was substituted, had been vitriolic about the Glazer family, Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Jason Wilcox. But United left the pitch in the relegation zone while their supporters serenaded Michael Carrick.

“It’s hard to believe it’s not Scholes,” they sang. In one respect, it was hard to believe it was not Sir Alex Ferguson, plucking results from nowhere. In another, it was hard to believe this was not the prelude to a sacking. It may still be.

But Carrick won’t quit. “That’s not going to happen,” he said. “I am quite clear what direction the club needs to go in and we need to win games.” They have only won once in 11 games, one point in three in the Premier League but Carrick is starting to specialise in escapology. Bournemouth had seemed the end for him, Roma looked it when his side were 2-0 down. Aston Villa seemed his valedictory game twice, before two two-goal comebacks.

“Making it hard for ourselves,” said Carrick. That was putting it mildly. Yet his side have twice delivered a show of spirit to salvage something from the brink of humiliation. Ferguson’s most famous comeback was delivered by two substitutes, Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. If Carrick has a lifeline now, it came from two replacements, scorers in Fergie Time, when it seemed time had run out for the latest United manager.

First Patrick Dorgu set up Joshua Zirkzee to halve the deficit. Then Dorgu headed in Bruno Fernandes’ 96th-minute corner. “In extra time conceding two goals is painful,” said Unai Emery. “Today we have lost two points.” Emery headed off for the tunnel when Dorgu scored, a picture of frustration. “I was angry with the situation, not with the players,” he said. A few minutes earlier, the Villa supporters had been jubilant, taunting their former midfielder Youri Tielemans with a chorus of: “Youri, what’s the score?”

Few, Emery included, foresaw the eventual answer. Villa were on course for their biggest victory at Old Trafford since 1920; then, suddenly, they did not have a win at all. This was confusing and complicated, crazy entertainment. United showed a self-destructive streak at the start of each half and reacted to spread the kind of chaos that put a smile back on their faces.

“I am disappointed we didn’t win the game,” claimed Carrick. United were both awful and exciting. They have character, if not competence at the back, where they did an impression of a particularly hungover pub team. A team with a series of historic lows have a pan-European level of porousness. As Villa scored four, no team in Europe’s five major leagues has conceded more goals in all competitions than United. Defensively, they are disastrous, disorganised, struggling at set-pieces, forever caught out by the counter-attack. Dalot is in hideous form and it got worse. Carrick erred by not swapping him with Noussair Mazraoui at half-time. What followed was all too predictable as, unable to contain the outstanding Alysson, Dalot fouled him to concede a penalty. Yet when Dalot eventually did go off, he was replaced by a rescuer, in the shape of the fit-again Dorgu.

Before his introduction, United had looked a shambles as they made a shocking start, and then another. They twice responded to Carrick’s team talks by capitulating, conceding two goals in four minutes at the start of the match and two in eight after the break.

Two goals behind after 18 minutes to Roma, United somehow surpassed that. This was the earliest they had ever been 2-0 down in a Premier League game when Villa doubled their lead, with Senne Lammens at fault for both.

Dalot should share the blame for Alyson’s first-minute opener, allowing the winger too much room to shoot. He beat the goalkeeper at his near post. When Lammens only pushed another Alysson shot straight to Nicolas Jackson, the summer signing slotted in his eighth goal in his last nine games.

It was, ridiculously, the fifth consecutive game in which United went 2-0 down. Briefly, they hinted at a second consecutive 3-2 win, only for something still more outlandish to unfold. The comeback against Roma began with a penalty won by Matheus Cunha and scored by Fernandes. Five days later, Boubacar Kamara fouled the Brazilian and the United captain sent Zion Suzuki the wrong way. Déjà vu.

As United were forced into a pattern of frenetic attacking, Cunha tried to power another fightback. There were echoes of Tuesday night, waves of attack. Cunha, Fernandes and Amad Diallo all came close. Suzuki made fine saves from Cunha and Amad. Tielemans swept in his first United goal from Mazraoui’s cutback.

After the interval, Villa felt fired up again. United emerged dopily. Carrick left Dalot up against the outstanding Alysson and tripped him. Either the winger was unstoppable or United made him look so but John McGinn, who missed his penalty against Fulham last week, scored this.

Then Lammens made his save of the game, sparing Leny Yoro an own goal but in vain. Jackson scuffed his shot but Leon Goretzka finished. His first Villa goal, it seemed, would finish off Carrick and United. Somehow, extraordinarily, it did not. They struck back in added time. His reign may be in added time, too.

#1082. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

This is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

It has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

#FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

The bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

On a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

The lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes

Updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager says the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta says: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a big favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

However, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.

Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Arteta kept Rice on the field for the full 90 minutes of Arsenal’s midweek victory over Slavia Prague but insisted the club is working harder than ever to manage the midfielder’s workload.

So far this season, Rice has been left out of Arsenal’s two Carabao Cup matches and also withdrew from the previous international break in September.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

“We are really looking after him more than any other season. The way he is training and all the love [he is being shown]. That’s it.

“Here are the demands of this football club and a player like him. Not only him, because there are many others that have even less time. That’s it. That has to be the mindset. If you start to put other things in your brain, [it will create] damage. Erase them, get them in the bin and just focus on what you have to do.”

Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.
